paragraphs.heading: A break in how we study nature
paragraphs.text: The Scientific Revolution was a change in European thought during the 16th and 17th centuries. It broke for good with the natural philosophy that came before, and it changed how people investigated and understood the natural world. The New Science that came out of it treated nature more like a machine, leaned more on mathematics, and centered on gathering and reading new evidence. Scholars widely treat it as the birth of modern science.

paragraphs.heading: Start and finish
paragraphs.text: The period is often dated from 1543, when two books appeared: Vesalius on the workings of the human body and Copernicus on the revolutions of the heavenly spheres. Some instead point to the supernova of 1572. It reached its peak in 1687, when Isaac Newton published his Principia.

paragraphs.heading: The old picture
paragraphs.text: In the 16th century the ideas of Aristotle still ruled European learning. His universe put the Earth at the center and was ranked in layers. At its middle was an imperfect earthly region of four elements, earth, water, air and fire, each seeking its natural place. Around it lay an unchanging heaven of nested spheres made of a fifth element, aether, moving only in perfect circles.

paragraphs.heading: Not built from nothing
paragraphs.text: The new physics and astronomy broke with this tradition, but they still grew out of it. Medieval scholars who recovered and debated ancient learning helped make the revolution possible. Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Newton all studied at universities founded in the High Middle Ages, and all admitted what they owed to earlier thinkers.

paragraphs.heading: Glass and print
paragraphs.text: Eyeglasses were first made in central Italy by about 1290, and Venetian glassmakers later produced a very clear glass called cristallo, used for lenses among other things. The first record of the telescope comes from a patent filed by a spectacle maker. Advances in making books also enabled the revolution. With Gutenberg's press, scholars in different countries could read the same texts and study the same diagrams, and compare their own observations with others'.

paragraphs.heading: A shock from the Americas
paragraphs.text: Most maps in 15th-century Europe followed Ptolemy's Geographia, which had no Americas on it at all. So the European arrival in the Americas came as a complete surprise. Because Europeans trusted Ptolemy on the stars as well as on maps, the discovery cast doubt on his astronomy too.
